statement.text: In geometric graph theory, the Hadwiger–Nelson problem, named after Hugo Hadwiger and Edward Nelson, asks for the minimum number of colors required to color the plane such that no two points at distance 1 from each other have the same color. The answer is unknown, but has been narrowed down to one of the numbers 5, 6 or 7. The correct value may depend on the choice of axioms for set theory.

claims.family_title: The Euclidean plane cannot be colored with five colors
claims.statement: Proves that every five-coloring of the Euclidean plane has a monochromatic pair at distance one, with no restriction on the color classes. This advances the Hadwiger–Nelson problem: together with the classical seven-coloring, only six and seven remain possible chromatic numbers of the plane.
claims.match_note: A lower bound of six. The chromatic number of the plane is six or seven.

formal.statement: The Hadwiger–Nelson problem asks for the fewest colors needed to color the plane so that points at distance one have different colors. The formalized results prove that five colors do not suffice and that seven colors do suffice. The lower bound applies to arbitrary colorings, with no measurability or continuity assumption; the upper bound includes every boundary point of the coloring regions.
